title: Git Stash & Worktrees: Parking Work Without Losing It
summary: A field guide to Git's two answers for context switching — stash for parking dirty work on a stack, worktrees for keeping multiple checkouts of one repo live at once. Covers the object-level mechanics, apply vs pop, worktree administration, and when each beats a plain branch switch.

chapters.title: The Context-Switch Problem
points: Working tree = files on disk you edit; index (staging area) = what `git add` recorded; HEAD = commit currently checked out. Three states, and stash/worktrees both manipulate them.

A branch switch (`git switch other`) refuses when local modifications would be overwritten: error 'Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout'. This is the trigger for stash or worktree.

Git actually allows a dirty switch when the modified files are identical between the two commits — it carries changes across. Failure only happens on conflicting paths, which is why the error feels random.
Four escape hatches: commit WIP, stash, a second worktree, or a second full clone. Each trades speed against isolation.
'Commit a WIP' pollutes history and forces `--amend`/rebase cleanup later; stash keeps history clean but hides work off-branch.
Stash is a stack of temporary commits inside the same working tree — one checkout, time-multiplexed.
Worktree is multiple working trees sharing one object database — many checkouts, space-multiplexed.
Rule of thumb: stash for interruptions measured in minutes; worktree for parallel work measured in hours or days.
Untracked and ignored files are the classic blind spot — neither branch switch nor plain `git stash` touches them by default.

chapters.title: Stash Basics: The Save/Restore Loop
points: `git stash` (alias for `git stash push`) rolls tracked modified + staged files back to HEAD and stores them on the stash stack.
`git stash push -m "wip: parser fix"` labels the entry; unlabeled entries get auto-message 'WIP on <branch>: <sha> <subject>' which becomes useless after three of them.
`git stash list` shows `stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`, … — index 0 is newest, indices renumber whenever an entry is dropped.
`git stash show stash@{1}` prints a diffstat; add `-p` for the full patch to inspect before restoring.
`git stash apply` restores contents and keeps the entry; `git stash pop` restores and deletes the entry.
`git stash drop stash@{2}` deletes one entry; `git stash clear` deletes all with no confirmation and no easy undo.
`git stash branch newbranch stash@{0}` creates a branch at the stash's parent commit, applies the stash there, drops it on success — the clean recovery for a stash that no longer applies.
Restore does not restore staging by default: staged changes come back unstaged unless you pass `--index`.
Stash is per-repository, not per-branch: a stash pushed on `feature-a` can be popped on `main`. Git will not warn you.

chapters.title: Stash Internals: It's Just Commits
points: Each stash entry is a real commit object with a magic shape — normally 2 parents, 3 with `-u`.
Parent 1 = HEAD at stash time (the base commit). Parent 2 = a commit holding the index/staged state. Parent 3 = a commit holding untracked files, present only when `-u`/`-a` used.
The stash commit's tree is the working-tree state; the second parent's tree is the index state. That split is why `--index` can restore staged/unstaged separation exactly.
The stack lives in `refs/stash`, a single ref. Older entries survive only in its reflog: `stash@{1}` literally means 'reflog entry 1 of refs/stash'.
Verify with `git log --graph --oneline refs/stash` or `git cat-file -p refs/stash` to see the parent list.
Because entries are reflog positions, indices shift: after `git stash drop stash@{0}`, old `stash@{1}` becomes `stash@{0}`. Scripts that hardcode indices break.
Stash commits are unreachable from any branch, so they are garbage-collection candidates once dropped — recovery window is `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`, default 30 days.
Recover a dropped stash: `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` then `git stash apply <sha>` or `git branch rescue <sha>`.
`git stash create` builds the stash commit and prints its SHA without touching the stack or the working tree — the scriptable primitive. `git stash store` pushes an existing SHA onto the stack.

chapters.title: apply vs pop: Choosing the Right One
points: `pop` = `apply` + `drop`, but only drops if apply succeeded cleanly.

Critical gotcha: if `pop` hits a merge conflict, the apply is partial AND the entry is kept. Resolving the conflict does not auto-drop it — you must `git stash drop` manually or you get a duplicate later.
`apply` is idempotent-friendly: use it to replay the same WIP onto two different branches (e.g. test a fix on `main` and on `release/2.x`).
Comparison row — safety: `apply` keeps a backup copy; `pop` deletes it. Prefer `apply` when the target branch has moved far from the stash base.
Comparison row — hygiene: `pop` prevents stack rot; `apply` grows a graveyard of stale entries you no longer trust.

Comparison row — conflict handling: after a conflicted `apply` you can `git checkout -- .` and retry; after a conflicted `pop` you can too, because the entry still exists. Both recoverable — the risk is the silent duplicate.
`--index` with either restores the staged/unstaged split; it fails outright if the index state cannot be reproduced, whereas plain apply degrades to 'everything unstaged'.
Applying a stash is a merge, not a patch application: Git 3-way merges the stash tree against the current HEAD, so it can succeed even when the file moved or context lines changed.
Practical default: `git stash apply`, verify the result builds, then `git stash drop`. Two commands, zero surprises.

chapters.title: Stash Flags Worth Knowing
points: `-u` / `--include-untracked`: also stashes untracked files (stored as the third parent). Without it, new files stay behind and can collide on the next branch.
`-a` / `--all`: stashes untracked AND ignored files. Dangerous around `node_modules/` or `build/` — it will happily stash gigabytes.

`-k` / `--keep-index`: stashes everything but leaves the staged version in the working tree. The classic pre-commit test: stage the change, `git stash push -k`, run tests on exactly what you're about to commit.
`--staged` (Git 2.35+): stashes only staged changes, leaving unstaged work alone — the inverse of `--keep-index`.
`git stash push -p` / `--patch`: interactively pick hunks to stash, splitting one messy edit into 'park this half, keep that half'.
Pathspec form: `git stash push -m msg -- src/parser.js src/lexer.js` stashes only those paths.
`git stash push` with no tracked changes exits with 'No local changes to save' and pushes nothing — check exit status in scripts.
Combining `-u` with a pathspec works; combining `--keep-index` with `--patch` does not do what most people expect — the kept index is the pre-stash index, not the selected hunks.

chapters.title: Worktrees: One Repo, Many Checkouts
points: `git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch` creates a second working directory checked out to `hotfix-branch`, sharing the original `.git` object database.
`git worktree add -b fix-123 ../fix-123` creates the branch and the worktree in one step; `git worktree add --detach ../scratch HEAD` gives a detached checkout for throwaway experiments.
The original checkout is the 'main worktree'; the rest are 'linked worktrees'. `git worktree list` shows all with path, HEAD sha, and branch.
Objects, refs, config, remotes, and hooks are shared — a `git fetch` in one worktree updates all of them. No re-clone, no re-fetch.
Disk cost is one working tree of files, not a second copy of history. On a repo with a large `.git`, that is a huge saving over a second clone.
`git worktree remove ../hotfix` deletes it cleanly; `git worktree prune` cleans up admin files after a directory was deleted manually.
`git worktree lock ../on-usb --reason "removable drive"` stops prune from reaping a worktree on unmounted or slow storage.
`git worktree move ../old ../new` relocates a worktree and fixes its internal path pointers — never just `mv` it.
Each worktree has its own HEAD, index, and stash-free working state, but the *stash stack is shared* via `refs/stash`, which surprises people.

chapters.title: Worktree Internals & Rules
points: A linked worktree's directory contains a `.git` *file* (not a directory) holding `gitdir: /path/to/repo/.git/worktrees/<name>`.
Per-worktree admin lives in `.git/worktrees/<name>/`: `HEAD`, `index`, `commondir`, `gitdir`, and its own reflogs.
`commondir` points back to the shared `.git`; everything not listed as per-worktree resolves there.
Per-worktree refs: `HEAD`, `refs/bisect/*`, `refs/worktree/*`. Everything else — branches, tags, remotes, `refs/stash` — is shared.

Hard rule: the same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees. Attempt gives 'fatal: <branch> is already checked out at <path>'. Override with `--force` only if you understand you now have two indexes racing on one ref.
`git worktree add` on an already-checked-out branch is the #1 error; the fix is usually `--detach` or a new branch.
`$GIT_DIR` differs per worktree, so scripts using `.git/` paths directly break — use `git rev-parse --git-dir` (worktree-specific) and `--git-common-dir` (shared).
`git config --worktree <key> <value>` sets a config value for one worktree only; requires `extensions.worktreeConfig=true`.
Submodules inside linked worktrees are historically fragile — verify before relying on them in a multi-worktree setup.
Deleting a worktree directory with `rm -rf` leaves a stale entry in `git worktree list` until you `prune`.

chapters.title: When Each Wins
points: Branch switch wins: clean tree, quick hop, you're done in the other branch and coming right back. Zero admin overhead.
Stash wins: 30-second interruption, small diff, same build artifacts, no long-running processes to restart.
Worktree wins: long-lived parallel work, expensive build/install state, running dev server, or you need both versions visible at once.
Killer worktree case — comparing two versions side by side: diff behavior, run both test suites, open both in the editor simultaneously. Stash cannot do this.

Killer worktree case — a build that takes 10 minutes: switching branches invalidates `node_modules`, `target/`, `__pycache__`, incremental compiler caches. A second worktree keeps each branch's build hot.
Killer worktree case — a long code review: check out the PR branch in `../review` without disturbing your in-progress feature.
Killer stash case — `git pull` refuses because of local noise: `git stash && git pull --rebase && git stash pop`.
Killer stash case — pre-commit verification with `--keep-index`: test exactly the staged change.
Worktree vs second clone: worktree shares objects and refs (cheap, one fetch); a clone gives full isolation including config and hooks (needed when a tool mutates repo config).
Anti-pattern: using stash as long-term storage. Anything you'd be sad to lose belongs on a branch, not on `refs/stash`.

chapters.title: Cost & Trade-offs
points: Stash push/pop cost is proportional to the size of the changed set, plus a tree write — effectively instant for typical diffs.
Stash storage cost: one commit + trees + blobs per entry, deduplicated against existing objects. Cheap unless you stash build output with `-a`.
Worktree add cost = one full checkout of the tree (I/O bound on file count), plus a few hundred bytes of admin files. No object copying.
Full clone cost = whole object database again; a 2 GB `.git` becomes 4 GB. `git clone --shared`/`--reference` avoids that but introduces a fragile dependency on the source repo.
Stash mental cost is the real cost: an unlabeled stack is opaque, and its entries carry no branch context.
Worktree mental cost: multiple directories to remember, editors/IDEs indexing each one, and tooling that assumes exactly one checkout.
`git gc` runs against the shared object store, so it must consider every worktree's HEAD and index as roots — this is why prune-before-gc hygiene matters.
Scaling: stash degrades badly past ~5 entries; worktrees degrade past ~5 directories mostly through disk and indexing pressure, not Git itself.
Concurrency: two worktrees can run `git status`/builds simultaneously; one working tree cannot. Some operations still take repo-wide locks on shared refs.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Fixes
points: Mistake: `git stash` then `git checkout` other branch then `git stash pop` — conflicts because the stash's base commit differs. Fix: `git stash branch <name>` to reapply on the original base.
Mistake: forgetting `-u`, then `git clean -fd` wipes the untracked files that were never stashed. Unrecoverable. Fix: default to `git stash push -u`.
Mistake: `git stash clear` to 'tidy up'. Entries become unreachable immediately; only `git fsck --unreachable` and the gc window save you.
Mistake: conflicted `pop`, resolve, commit, then later `pop` the still-present entry and reapply the same change on top. Fix: check `git stash list` right after resolving a conflicted pop.
Mistake: assuming the stash belongs to the branch you made it on. It doesn't — always read `git stash list`'s 'WIP on <branch>' text before popping.
Mistake: `rm -rf ../worktree-dir` instead of `git worktree remove`. Leaves stale admin state; fix with `git worktree prune`.
Mistake: `git worktree add ../x main` while `main` is checked out in the main worktree. Fix: `--detach`, or make a new branch off `main`.
Mistake: pointing a build script at `.git/hooks` or `.git/config` via a hardcoded relative path — breaks in linked worktrees. Fix: `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`.
Mistake: deleting a branch that a linked worktree has checked out. Git blocks it; force-deleting leaves that worktree on an orphaned ref.
Mistake: treating `git stash pop` as atomic in a script. It is not — check the exit code and inspect `git stash list` afterward.

chapters.title: Recipes
points: Interruption: `git stash push -u -m "wip: checkout flow"` → fix the bug → commit → `git stash pop`.
Test only the staged change: `git add -p` → `git stash push --keep-index -m "unstaged rest"` → run tests → commit → `git stash pop`.
Move work to the right branch: `git stash -u` → `git switch -c correct-branch` → `git stash pop`.
Rescue a stash that no longer applies: `git stash branch salvage stash@{0}` → merge or cherry-pick from `salvage`.
Recover a dropped stash: `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` → `git show <sha>` to identify → `git stash apply <sha>`.
Review a PR without disturbing your work: `git fetch origin pull/123/head:pr-123` → `git worktree add ../review pr-123` → review → `git worktree remove ../review`.
Emergency hotfix with a hot build: `git worktree add -b hotfix-501 ../hotfix origin/main` → fix, test, push → `git worktree remove ../hotfix`.
Side-by-side comparison: `git worktree add ../v1 v1.0` and `git worktree add ../v2 v2.0`, then run both and diff outputs.
Bisect without losing your workspace: `git worktree add ../bisect --detach` → run `git bisect` there (bisect refs are per-worktree).
Clean sweep: `git worktree list` → `git worktree remove` each finished one → `git worktree prune` → `git stash list` and clear the graveyard deliberately.

chapters.title: Summary & Decision Table
points: Stash = a stack of hidden 2-or-3-parent commits under `refs/stash`, indexed by reflog position, in one working tree.
Worktree = an extra working directory with its own HEAD and index, backed by the shared object store, listed in `.git/worktrees/`.
`apply` keeps the entry, `pop` drops it on success only — after any conflict, verify `git stash list` yourself.
Decision row — interruption under 10 minutes, small diff: stash.
Decision row — parallel work, expensive build state, or side-by-side comparison: worktree.
Decision row — need isolated config/hooks or a different remote: separate clone.
Decision row — clean tree, just moving around: plain `git switch`.
Always label stashes (`-m`) and always include untracked (`-u`); the defaults are the source of most stash pain.
Never treat `refs/stash` as storage — promote anything valuable to a branch with `git stash branch`.
Always remove worktrees with `git worktree remove`, and `prune` after any manual directory deletion.
One-line recall: stash time-multiplexes one tree; worktrees space-multiplex many trees over one history.
